title: AI Discovery in Combinatorics: From Problems to Solutions and Back
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 12 Oct 2026]
Title:AI Discovery in Combinatorics: From Problems to Solutions and Back to Bigger Problems
View PDF
            Abstract:We introduce $qt$Bench, a benchmark of 29 open problems in algebraic combinatorics. These problems ask for a simple combinatorial algorithm that explains given polynomial coefficients or identities. To help AI agents search for such algorithms, we provide a scaffold for playing with combinatorial objects, countering cheating attempts, and testing candidate solutions. To explore how far frontier AI systems can go on these problems, we collaborated with OpenAI, whose researchers obtained proposed solutions to several of them. This highlights bigger meta-problems: is AI discovery at scale ethical? How should these results be released? How should proof digestion be organized? We discuss these questions and give our views.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper releases qtBench, 29 open algebraic-combinatorics problems for AI agents, reports partial solutions found with OpenAI, and raises ethics-of-discovery questions.
report.background: Combinatorics has become the favoured proving ground for AI mathematics because answers are cheap to check yet hard to find: a claimed algorithm either reproduces the coefficients or it does not. Since DeepMind's FunSearch produced new cap-set constructions and AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry scored at olympiad level, attention has shifted from contest problems to genuine open research questions. Benchmarks such as FrontierMath and the Erdős-problems community have normalised feeding unsolved maths to frontier models, but most efforts stop at a score. This paper instead bundles a scaffold for manipulating combinatorial objects, anti-cheating checks and automated testing, then pairs the benchmark with an industrial lab. The result is less a leaderboard than a case study in what happens when a model produces something that looks like new mathematics and nobody yet knows how to absorb it.
key_points: The benchmark covers 29 open problems in algebraic combinatorics, each asking for a simple combinatorial algorithm that explains a given polynomial coefficient or identity. That format makes success objectively checkable: the algorithm must generate the data rather than merely describe it.

The authors ship a scaffold, not just questions. It gives AI agents a sandbox for experimenting with combinatorial objects and includes counter-measures against cheating attempts, such as models pattern-matching answers or exploiting the test harness instead of solving the problem.

OpenAI researchers collaborated on the effort and obtained proposed solutions to several problems. The paper is careful to frame these as proposals requiring verification and digestion, not settled theorems, which itself signals how unsettled the norms around such results still are.

The paper pivots from results to meta-problems: whether AI-driven discovery at scale is ethical, how findings should be released and credited, and how the community should organise the human labour of checking machine-written proofs.
It is explicitly a benchmark-and-position paper, arguing that evaluation design, verification pipelines and release policy must be built alongside the models, rather than improvised after the fact.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this sets a template where a benchmark is bundled with a verification harness and a lab partnership, shifting competition from raw scores to defensible, checkable results. For mathematicians, the scarce resource becomes proof digestion — reading, verifying and generalising machine proposals — which implies new roles and review infrastructure. For developers, the interesting artefact is the scaffold: sandboxing, anti-gaming checks and automated testing for open-ended reasoning tasks generalise well beyond combinatorics. For regular users, expect more headlines claiming AI solved a maths problem, and more caveats about what 'solved' means. The paper's ethical framing may also push labs toward staged disclosure, delaying publication until human verification catches up.
report.tools: Watch qtBench and its scaffold as they appear on arXiv and likely Hugging Face; Lean 4 with Mathlib for formal verification of candidate proofs; DeepMind's FunSearch codebase as the reference pattern for LLM-plus-evaluator search; AlphaProof for olympiad-style proving; the FrontierMath benchmark for broader coverage; and the Erdős Problems site for open-problem tracking.
